subject: ela
intro: Strong readers do two things with a text. First, they explain what the author says right on the page, using the exact words as proof. That is an explicit detail. Second, they draw inferences, which are smart guesses the author does not state but leaves clues for. To make a good inference, add what the text says to what you already know, then point back to the detail that led you there. Whether the answer is stated or hinted, always refer to the specific detail or example that proves it.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

At the edge of the field, Marisol crouched behind the tall grass and did not move. Her heart pounded as the deer stepped closer, one careful hoof at a time. She had waited two hours for this exact moment, and she slowly raised her camera without making a sound.

What is Marisol trying to do, and which detail tells you?

steps: Notice she stays still, waits, and raises a camera.
The phrase "she slowly raised her camera without making a sound" is the key detail.
Someone raising a camera quietly at an animal is trying to photograph it, not hunt or scare it.
solution.answer: Marisol is trying to take a photograph of the deer. The story says "she slowly raised her camera without making a sound," which shows she wants a picture and does not want to frighten the deer away.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

The first day at his new school, Owen ate lunch alone at the end of a long table. He kept glancing at a group laughing near the window, then looking back down at his tray. When a girl named Priya waved him over, he grabbed his tray so fast that his milk nearly tipped.

How did Owen most likely feel before Priya waved, and which details show it?

steps: Find the explicit details: he ate "alone," kept "glancing" at the laughing group, then looked "back down."
Add what you know: a person who eats alone and keeps looking at others often feels left out or lonely.
His fast, eager move when invited confirms he wanted to join all along.
solution.answer: Owen most likely felt lonely and left out. The details that he "ate lunch alone," kept "glancing at a group laughing," and then grabbed his tray "so fast" when invited show he wanted company but did not know how to join.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Grandma Rose never threw anything away. In her sewing room, buttons filled old jam jars, and scraps of bright cloth spilled from every drawer. "One day," she always said, "each little piece finds its place." When my coat ripped the night before the concert, she stitched a patch shaped like a star, and I was the only kid there with a coat like a piece of the sky.

steps: The question is missing, so read for the main point the narrator makes.
Grandma saves scraps and says "each little piece finds its place."
The saved cloth becomes the star patch that fixes the coat, proving her saying true.
solution.answer: The story shows that Grandma Rose's habit of saving scraps has a purpose. Her saying "each little piece finds its place" is proven when a saved scrap becomes the star patch that repairs the narrator's coat.

items.prompt:
Read the poem.

The old dog waits beside the door,
His leash still hanging on the hook.
He lifts his head at every car,
Then sighs and gives the road a look.

What can you infer about the dog, and which line supports it?

steps: Explicit details: he waits by the door, lifts his head at every car, then sighs.
Add what you know: waiting near the leash and reacting to each car means he hopes someone will come.
The sigh after each car shows disappointment, so he is waiting and hoping.
solution.answer: You can infer the dog is waiting hopefully for someone to come home or take him out. The line "He lifts his head at every car, then sighs" shows he hopes at each car and feels let down when no one comes.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Devon had practiced his violin piece a hundred times, but on stage his bow trembled. He looked out and found his little sister in the third row, holding up the paper heart she had drawn for him. His shoulders dropped, his breath slowed, and the first clear note rang out.

What helped Devon calm down, and which detail proves it?

steps: Find the turning point: his bow trembled until he saw his sister and her paper heart.
Right after seeing her, "his shoulders dropped, his breath slowed."
Those changes show her support calmed him.
solution.answer: Seeing his little sister holding up the paper heart helped Devon calm down. The detail that right after, "his shoulders dropped, his breath slowed, and the first clear note rang out" proves her support settled his nerves.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

The lighthouse keeper, Mr. Ansel, climbed the spiral stairs every evening at dusk. That winter his knees ached and the steps felt endless, but he never missed a night. "Ships out there are counting on this light," he told the gulls, "and a promise is a promise."

Why does Mr. Ansel keep climbing even when it hurts? Use a detail from the text.

steps: His knees ache, yet he never misses a night.
He explains his reason out loud to the gulls.
He believes ships depend on the light and that a promise must be kept.
solution.answer: Mr. Ansel keeps climbing because he feels responsible for the ships that depend on the light. He says, "Ships out there are counting on this light, and a promise is a promise," which shows duty is why he does not miss a night.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

When the science fair ribbons were handed out, Talia did not win. She clapped hardest of all for Reuben, whose bridge had held the most weight. Later, she pulled out her notebook and wrote at the top of a fresh page: "Next year, test the joints first."

What can you infer about Talia's attitude toward losing? Support your answer with a detail.

steps: Explicit details: she clapped hardest for the winner and wrote a plan for next year.
Add what you know: someone who cheers a rival and plans improvements is not bitter.
She treats the loss as a chance to learn.
solution.answer: Talia has a positive, growth-minded attitude about losing. She "clapped hardest of all" for the winner and wrote "Next year, test the joints first," showing she uses the loss to plan and improve instead of feeling bitter.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

The map Aunt Frida gave me was soft and torn at the folds, with tiny notes crammed in the margins in three different colors of ink. A coffee ring circled the harbor town. Near the mountains someone had written, "Do not trust the shortcut." I traced the worn path with my finger and understood that this map had traveled far before it reached me.

What does the condition of the map tell the narrator, and which details lead to that idea?

steps: Explicit details: torn folds, notes in three ink colors, a coffee ring, a warning about a shortcut.
Add what you know: wear, many notes, and stains build up only after long, repeated use.
So the map has been used and carried by people over a long time.
solution.answer: The worn condition tells the narrator the map has been used and carried for a long time by others. Details like "torn at the folds," "notes... in three different colors of ink," and a "coffee ring" show years of use, which is why the narrator says it "had traveled far before it reached me."

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Every player on the team got a jersey except Nadia, whose last name had been left off the order by mistake. She wore her plain gray shirt to the first game and cheered louder than anyone from the bench. When the coach finally handed her the missing jersey weeks later, she folded it neatly and said, "I already felt like part of the team."

Ask one question that is answered explicitly in the text and one that requires an inference. Answer both, citing details.

steps: An explicit question: Why did Nadia not get a jersey at first? The text states her name "had been left off the order by mistake."
An inference question: How does Nadia feel about belonging? She is not stated to feel hurt.
Her cheering and her line "I already felt like part of the team" support that she felt included regardless of the jersey.
solution.answer: Explicit: 'Why did Nadia not get a jersey?' The text says her name "had been left off the order by mistake." Inference: 'Does Nadia feel like she belongs?' Yes. She "cheered louder than anyone" and said, "I already felt like part of the team," showing belonging did not depend on the jersey.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

The storm had knocked branches all over the trail. Instead of turning back, the twins dragged the largest limbs to the side, stacking them into a neat pile. By the time the ranger arrived, the path was clear. "We figured someone had to," said one twin, wiping mud from her hands.

Write a short explanation of what kind of people the twins are, using at least two details from the text as evidence.

steps: Explicit details: they did not turn back, they dragged limbs aside and stacked them, and one said "someone had to."
Add what you know: people who clear a path for others without being asked are helpful and responsible.
Cite two details to support the trait.
solution.answer: The twins are helpful and responsible. Evidence one: "Instead of turning back," they "dragged the largest limbs to the side." Evidence two: one twin said, "We figured someone had to," showing they cleared the trail for others on their own.
